title: Episode 155: William McKinley: The Front Porch Campaign and 'A Splendid Little War' (1896–1898)

In 1896, the United States faced an epic ideological showdown that defined modern American politics. In one corner was William Jennings Bryan, the youthful populist crusader who barnstormed eighteen thousand miles across the nation. In the other was William McKinley—the calm, dignified Civil War veteran from Canton, Ohio, who conducted the legendary 'Front Porch Campaign' masterminded by Mark Hanna, speaking to three-quarters of a million citizens who traveled to his lawn. Winning the presidency on a platform of prosperity and sound money, McKinley was soon confronted by global catastrophe: the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor. Reluctantly thrust into the Spanish-American War, McKinley presided over 'a splendid little war' that dismantled the Spanish Empire in one hundred days and transformed the United States into a global superpower. Discover the rise of William McKinley.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the watershed presidency of William McKinley. Standing at the threshold between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, McKinley brought an end to decades of economic paralysis and presided over the dramatic emergence of the United States as a premier global power. Here is George with the full story of the Front Porch Campaign and the war that reshaped the world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MAJOR FROM NILES
William McKinley was the last American president to have fought in the Civil War. Born in 1843 in Niles, Ohio, the seventh of nine children of an iron foundry manager, McKinley was an eighteen-year-old schoolteacher when Confederate guns opened fire on Fort Sumter. He enlisted immediately as a private in the 23rd Ohio Volunteer Infantry, serving under future president Rutherford B. Hayes. At the horrific Battle of Antietam in September 1862—the bloodiest single day in American history—nineteen-year-old Sergeant McKinley performed an act of legendary gallantry. Under a devastating hail of Confederate artillery and rifle fire, McKinley loaded two mules with barrels of hot coffee and rations, driving his supply wagon directly onto the smoking front line to feed his exhausted, starving comrades.\n\nHayes wrote in his diary that McKinley was the coolest man under fire he had ever seen, securing him a battlefield promotion to second lieutenant. By war's end, McKinley had been brevetted major for gallantry at Cedar Creek. Returning to Ohio, he studied law, married the frail, devoted Ida Saxton, and climbed the political ladder to Congress and the governorship of Ohio. Known for his dignified, immaculate dress, calm temperament, and personal kindness, McKinley was universally beloved across Ohio, earning the affectionate title 'The Major.'\n\nMcKinley's Civil War heroism at Antietam reflected his lifelong conviction that leadership was defined by humble service and steady courage under pressure.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: MARK HANNA AND THE FRONT PORCH OF CANTON
In 1896, McKinley secured the Republican nomination for president, paired with the genius of Marcus Alonzo Hanna—a wealthy Cleveland iron merchant who became the first modern political campaign manager. Facing them was the dynamic thirty-six-year-old Democratic nominee, William Jennings Bryan, who electrified the nation with his radical crusade for the free coinage of silver. Bryan boarded private trains and barnstormed eighteen thousand miles across twenty-seven states, delivering up to thirty fiery speeches a day to millions of people.\n\nRather than try to match Bryan's frantic travels, Mark Hanna devised a brilliant, unprecedented strategy: the 'Front Porch Campaign.' McKinley stayed home at his modest Victorian house on North Market Street in Canton, Ohio. Hanna organized the American railroad network to offer subsidized, cheap excursion tickets to Canton. Over four months, more than seven hundred and fifty thousand citizens—delegations of union laborers, coal miners, Civil War veterans, farmers, and women's clubs—traveled to Canton from every state in the Union. Standing on his wooden front porch beneath an American flag, McKinley greeted each delegation with quiet dignity, delivering calm, reasoned addresses advocating sound money, protective tariffs, and national prosperity. McKinley won an overwhelming victory, breaking twenty-four years of political stalemate and launching thirty years of Republican dominance.\n\nThe Front Porch campaign demonstrated the power of organized public relations, setting the pattern for twentieth-century presidential communications.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SHADOW OF CUBA AND THE SINKING OF THE MAINE
Taking office in March 1897, McKinley was determined to focus entirely on domestic economic recovery. But ninety miles off the coast of Florida, a humanitarian catastrophe was unfolding. The island of Cuba had erupted in a brutal war of independence against Spanish colonial rule. Spanish General Valeriano Weyler instituted the ruthless 'reconcentrado' policy, herding hundreds of thousands of rural Cuban civilians into barbed-wire concentration camps, where over two hundred thousand died of starvation and disease. In New York, rival sensationalist newspapers owned by William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer published graphic, screaming headlines demanding American intervention to liberate Cuba.\n\nMcKinley, who remembered the slaughter of Antietam, was deeply reluctant to enter war: 'I have been through one war,' McKinley told friends. 'I have seen the dead piled high, and I do not want to see another.' To protect American citizens and property in Havana, McKinley dispatched the second-class battleship USS Maine on a friendly visit in January 1898. On the calm, humid evening of February 15, 1898, catastrophe struck. A colossal explosion ripped through the forward hull of the Maine, igniting five tons of powder magazines and destroying the ship. Two hundred and sixty-six American sailors were killed, their bodies blown into the dark waters of Havana Harbor.\n\nThe horrific suffering of Cuban civilians under General Weyler's reconcentration policy deeply moved the American public, creating overwhelming pressure for humanitarian intervention.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: 'REMEMBER THE MAINE, TO HELL WITH SPAIN!'
The destruction of the Maine unleashed an uncontrollable firestorm of war fever across the United States. Hearst's New York Journal offered a fifty-thousand-dollar reward for the perpetrator, shouting in red ink that Spanish saboteurs had torpedoed the ship. Across the country, patriotic rallies erupted, and citizens wore buttons proclaiming: 'Remember the Maine, to Hell with Spain!' A naval court of inquiry concluded that the ship had been destroyed by an external submarine mine, though modern naval investigations suggest an accidental spontaneous combustion in the coal bunker next to the magazine was the likely cause.\n\nMcKinley attempted to negotiate a peaceful settlement, demanding that Spain declare an immediate armistice and close the reconcentration camps. Spain made major concessions, but refused to surrender Cuban independence. Young hawks in the administration—most notably Assistant Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt—accused McKinley of cowardice, Roosevelt privately complaining that 'McKinley has no more backbone than a chocolate éclair.' Recognizing that Congress was prepared to declare war over his head, McKinley bowed to the inevitable. On April 11, 1898, McKinley sent a war message to Capitol Hill, declaring that the war was a neutral intervention in the cause of humanity.\n\nMcKinley exhausted every diplomatic channel to avoid bloodshed, agreeing to military action only when Spanish concessions proved too little and too late to prevent catastrophe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: DEWEY AT MANILA BAY AND THE 100-DAY WAR
What followed was, in the famous words of American ambassador to London John Hay, 'a splendid little war.' The conflict lasted just one hundred and thirteen days, resulting in an astonishing, total American triumph. The war opened not in the Caribbean, but on the far side of the globe in the Pacific. On May 1, 1898, Commodore George Dewey steamed his Asiatic Squadron into Manila Bay in the Spanish colony of the Philippines. At dawn, Dewey turned calmly to the captain of his flagship Olympia and uttered the immortal order: 'You may fire when you are ready, Gridley.' In less than six hours, Dewey's modern steel cruisers completely pulverized the entire Spanish Pacific fleet without the loss of a single American sailor.\n\nIn Cuba, seventeen thousand American soldiers landed in June, including the colorful 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry—the 'Rough Riders'—led by Colonel Leonard Wood and Lieutenant Colonel Theodore Roosevelt. On July 1, Roosevelt led his men in a legendary, blood-soaked charge up Kettle Hill and San Juan Heights outside Santiago. Two days later, the United States Navy intercepted the Spanish Atlantic fleet attempting to escape Santiago Harbor, sinking or grounding every single Spanish warship. Spanish land forces surrendered shortly thereafter, and on August 12, 1898, Spain signed a peace protocol.\n\nThe astonishing naval victories at Manila Bay and Santiago established the United States Navy as a world-class maritime power capable of global power projection.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TREATY OF PARIS AND THE IMPERIAL DILEMMA
The Spanish-American War transformed the geopolitical map of the world. Under the Treaty of Paris signed in December 1898, Spain granted Cuba its independence, ceded the Caribbean island of Puerto Rico to the United States, and surrendered the Pacific island of Guam. But the fate of the vast Philippine archipelago—consisting of over seven thousand islands and eight million inhabitants—presented a profound moral and constitutional dilemma for President McKinley.\n\nMcKinley later recounted walking the floors of the White House night after night until midnight, praying for divine guidance: 'I went down on my knees and prayed to Almighty God for light and guidance. And one night late it came to me this way... that we could not give them back to Spain—that would be cowardly and dishonorable; that we could not turn them over to France or Germany—our commercial rivals in the Orient—that would be bad business and discreditable; that we could not leave them to themselves—they were unfit for self-government; and that there was nothing left for us to do but to take them all, and to educate the Filipinos, and uplift and civilize and Christianize them.' The United States agreed to pay Spain twenty million dollars for the Philippines. For the first time in its history, the American Republic had acquired an overseas empire.\n\nThe debate over the annexation of the Philippines ignited a profound constitutional debate about the nature of the American Republic and the perils of overseas imperialism.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE DAWN OF THE AMERICAN CENTURY
The acquisition of an overseas empire ignited a fierce national debate between imperialists and anti-imperialists, including Mark Twain, Andrew Carnegie, and Grover Cleveland, who argued that governing colonial subjects without their consent violated the Declaration of Independence. Yet the American public overwhelmingly embraced the new global stature. Under William McKinley's steady hand, the United States annexed the Republic of Hawaii in 1898, established the visionary 'Open Door Policy' in China to guarantee equal trade access and preserve Chinese territorial integrity, and dispatched American troops to rescue foreign legations during the Boxer Rebellion of 1900.\n\nAt home, the economy was booming: factories operated around the clock, American exports surpassed European competitors for the first time, and the gold standard was permanently codified in law with the Gold Standard Act of 1900. When voters went to the polls in November 1900, they resoundingly reelected William McKinley in an even larger landslide than 1896, rewarding him for four years of 'the Full Dinner Pail.' At his side as Vice President was the national war hero, Theodore Roosevelt. McKinley stood at the absolute zenith of power and popular acclaim. But as the new century dawned, a dark shadow was gathering in the industrial alleys of Cleveland.\n\nMcKinley's reelection in 1900 affirmed the nation's confidence in his steady leadership, ushering in an era of unprecedented industrial growth and international influence.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
William McKinley's first administration propelled the United States out of isolation and onto the world stage as a premier global power. His calm, consensus-building leadership laid the foundation for the American Century. Next week, we examine the tragic conclusion of McKinley's life: the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, the anarchist Leon Czolgosz, and the fateful handshake at the Temple of Music that elevated Theodore Roosevelt to the presidency. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
